title: Where do superheroes come from?
subtitle: From Hercules to Superman
subject: litterature
description: Superman, Wonder Woman, Shazam and Marvel's Thor are barely a century old. The figures behind them, Hercules, the Amazons, Samson and the god of thunder, are thousands of years old.
author: elizabeth-singer-hunt

hero.hook: Under Superman's cape and Wonder Woman's costume hide heroes three thousand years old.

blocks.text: Thousands of years before Superman or Marvel's Thor, the Greeks and Romans were already telling stories of characters with superhuman powers. [[Heracles]], better known by his Roman name, Hercules, was a son of **Zeus** famed for his strength and his seemingly impossible labors. **Achilles**, the greatest warrior of Homer's *Iliad*, fought like no one else, and the [[Amazons]], led by their queen Hippolyta, embodied the woman warrior.

Twentieth-century comic-book creators drew on these tales to shape **Wonder Woman** or **Captain Marvel**, also known as Shazam. These heroes are modern, but some of the ideas behind them go back to stories several millennia old. So where do superheroes really come from?

sections.title: Shazam, a magic word from antiquity

blocks.text: The arrival of Superman transformed comic books. Created by writer Jerry Siegel and artist Joe Shuster, he debuted in *Action Comics* #1 in **1938** and became a sensation: the genre was born. Other publishers wanted a superhero of their own. At [[Fawcett Comics]], writer Bill Parker first imagined a team of heroes, each with the power of a different mythological figure, before combining those powers in a single character drawn by C. C. Beck: **Billy Batson**.

Billy debuted as Captain Marvel in *Whiz Comics* #2, in **1940**. The boy turned into an adult superhero by shouting "Shazam!" The magic word held an ancient secret: it was an acronym for the **six figures** whose powers he inherited. The wisdom of Solomon, the strength of Hercules, the stamina of Atlas, the power of Zeus, the courage of Achilles and the speed of Mercury. Solomon was a biblical king; the others came from Greek and Roman mythology.

sections.title: Wonder Woman, daughter of the Amazons

blocks.text: Wonder Woman was born in **1941**, drawn by Harry G. Peter from an idea by the psychologist William Moulton Marston. She became a powerful female superhero and a role model around the world. Her creator deliberately rooted her story in Greek mythology: her mother is **Hippolyta**, Queen of the Amazons. Enslaved and chained by Hercules, the Amazons eventually broke free and built their own society.

blocks.caption: Heracles fighting the Amazons, Attic black-figure amphora from the 6th century BC.

blocks.text: Her indestructible cuffs recall those chains: a reminder of captivity became the very weapon she used to deflect bullets. Her arrival in the middle of **World War II** was no accident. In a society in upheaval, Marston wanted her to serve as "psychological propaganda for the new type of woman." She fought the Axis powers, while her civilian alter ego, **Diana Prince**, worked for U.S. military intelligence.

Eighty-five years later, the Smithsonian Institution calls her the best-known and longest-lasting female superhero. Television series, films, video games: she remains an international symbol of women's strength.

Classical mythology was not the only ancient source for superheroes. Their creators also turned to the Bible. Jerry Siegel himself named [[Samson]], the strongman of the Old Testament, as a major influence on **Superman**. Both possessed extraordinary strength, and early Superman stories compared him directly to Samson.

blocks.caption: Samson Slaying the Lion, by Lucas Cranach the Elder, around 1525.

blocks.text: Sent to Earth from **Krypton**, his doomed planet, Superman grew up as Clark Kent before becoming the protector of Metropolis. Extraordinary strength and speed, then flight: he put his powers to work fighting crime and injustice. When he appeared in 1938, the ancient idea of the superhuman hero entered the modern age.

Superman's origin has also been compared to that of Moses: two infants sent away by their parents to escape destruction, raised by adoptive families and destined for great things. But Siegel never named Moses as an inspiration.

sections.title: Thor, a Norse god at Marvel

blocks.text: In the early 1960s, [[Stan Lee]] was helping create a new generation of Marvel heroes: the Fantastic Four in **1961**, the Hulk in **1962**. He wanted "something different and bigger than anything else" and asked himself "what could be bigger than a god?" Greek and Roman gods were already familiar, so he turned to Norse mythology.

With his brother Larry Lieber and artist **Jack Kirby**, he reinvented Thor, son of Odin and wielder of the hammer [[Mjölnir]], in *Journey into Mystery* #83, in **1962**. Odin, Loki and Asgard followed him into the Marvel universe. The god of thunder thus traveled from Scandinavian myth to comic books, then to Hollywood blockbusters.

Perhaps that is why today's superheroes feel both new and strangely familiar. For thousands of years, storytellers have invented extraordinary heroes to inspire us and to show us how to find the courage to confront evil, whatever form it takes.
